body:
You are drafting short lines of game text for a single-player D&D 2024 computer RPG set in Curse of Strahd's Barovia. Reply in plain text only. Do not message, route to, or ask anyone else; finish with your reply.

HOUSE RULES FOR ALL LINES
- ALLUDE, NEVER QUOTE. This game winks at another famous fantasy game in small ways, but no line may contain a name, quote, or catchphrase from another game, and no line may mention a game, a player, dice, rolls, levels or saving. Everything happens inside the world.
- The tone is gothic, dry and quietly funny, never cruel. The joke is in what is there.
- Give TWO options for every line so the editor can choose. Label each option A or B.
- Spoken lines are formatted: Speaker [mood]: Text   (mood optional: neutral, smile, angry, afraid, sad, sly, weary). One or two sentences a line.
THE NARRATOR (voice rules): an old gothic storyteller, fond of the party the way a gravedigger is fond of the weather: interested, no illusions. Second person, present tense ("You crouch..."), or the acting hero as {name}. One or two sentences; the second is usually the turn. Concrete senses, not adjectives. Never tells the player what to feel. No modern slang. When an animal speaks through the Speak with Animals spell, the Narrator reports it in quotes, in plain animal pictures (a dog says "the digger-man", "the box-maker").
CAMP TALKS: the party camps at night; a companion asks for a word. Companion lines are written "Name: text" (their own voice). The player picks short replies (write each as "> reply text") and each reply gets one or two lines of answer. Keep every line one or two sentences.

THISTLE: human ranger raised by her grandfather in the wild, loud, laughs with her whole body; short blunt plain words, rough grammar (never baby-talk); talks to animals as equals; pet phrases "Grandda says...", "Smells wrong.", "Bark and bones!" (her only oath), "Again!", "Mine." Real lines: "Stone boxes, again. Fine. But I'm sleeping on the roof." / "Grandda says a wolf that walks like a man is two kinds of trouble and one kind of sad."
WREN: halfling monk, ex-entertainer: fast, wry, chatty, London; one-liners; deflects with jokes until he doesn't; quotes his old master Sorrel; pet phrases "Easy." "Watch this." "Rude." "I'll allow it."

TALK 1, THISTLE AND THE BEAR. Earlier, the party helped Lavinia, a Vistani dancer at Tser Pool, whose dancing bear Bujor broke his chain to save a cub; he either came home to the stage with the cub (HOME) or went into the woods with it (WOODS). Thistle has been thinking about Bujor more than is normal. She confides, gruff and a bit embarrassed, that she likes him: big, warm, smells right, dances, never pulls on his chain; if he ever got tired of Lavinia... She asks the party not to tell anyone. It is sweet and funny, never crude.
Write: 3 Thistle opening lines (one with a HOME and a WOODS version of the same beat), then three replies with her answer to each:
> tease her (she laughs and throws a pine cone)
> tell her he'd be lucky (she goes quiet, pleased)
> promise not to tell (she makes you swear on something, Grandda style)

TALK 2, WREN'S UNFINISHED SONG. Wren has half a song he learned from a horned girl on a road far from here, a travelling bard who could never finish it; he hums the tune at night. He asks the party to help him finish the last verse. The verse has three lines; for EACH line the party picks one of three: hopeful, grim, or silly. Then Wren sings the finished verse at the fire, and the camp goes quiet, then cheers. Our own lyrics: about a road home through the dark, about friends who stayed. No lyric may be a real song's line. Each lyric line under 12 words; lines 1 to 3 should rhyme or half-rhyme (A/A/A, or AAB) whichever choices are picked, so keep the rhyme sound shared across the three options for each line.
Write:
- 2 Wren lines: the ask (the horned girl, the unfinished verse).
- LINE 1 options: hopeful / grim / silly.
- LINE 2 options: hopeful / grim / silly.
- LINE 3 options: hopeful / grim / silly.
- 1 Narrator line as Wren sings it at the fire (the verse itself is shown separately).
- 2 Wren lines afterwards: delighted, one serious line about the girl ("wherever she is, I hope someone finished it for her too").
- 1 NARRATOR line for the inn at Vallaki, a night after: someone downstairs plays Wren's song badly and the whole room joins in on the last line. One sentence, under 30 words.

Return in this layout (A/B options as before for every spoken or narrated line; the lyric options need no A/B):
T1-OPEN-1A: Thistle: ...
T1-OPEN-1B: Thistle: ...
T1-OPEN-2-HOME-A: Thistle: ...
T1-OPEN-2-WOODS-A: Thistle: ...
T1-OPEN-2-HOME-B: Thistle: ...
T1-OPEN-2-WOODS-B: Thistle: ...
T1-OPEN-3A: Thistle: ...
T1-OPEN-3B: Thistle: ...
T1-TEASE: > ... | Thistle: ...
T1-LUCKY: > ... | Thistle: ...
T1-PROMISE: > ... | Thistle: ...
T2-ASK-A: Wren: ... | Wren: ...
T2-ASK-B: Wren: ... | Wren: ...
L1: hopeful: ... | grim: ... | silly: ...
L2: hopeful: ... | grim: ... | silly: ...
L3: hopeful: ... | grim: ... | silly: ...
T2-SING-A: Narrator: ...
T2-SING-B: Narrator: ...
T2-AFTER-A: Wren: ... | Wren: ...
T2-AFTER-B: Wren: ... | Wren: ...
INN-A: Narrator: ...
INN-B: Narrator: ...
result:
T1-OPEN-1A: Thistle [weary]: Can't sleep with the mist pressing on my neck. Keep thinking on Lavinia's big brown bear back at Tser Pool.
T1-OPEN-1B: Thistle [neutral]: You still awake? My head's stuck on that dancing bear of Lavinia's, big Bujor.
T1-OPEN-2-HOME-A: Thistle [smile]: Big fellow like that, smells right, steps neat to the fiddle, and never once yanks his chain even with the cub at his heel. If he ever gets tired of Lavinia's wagon, he can share my fire.
T1-OPEN-2-WOODS-A: Thistle [smile]: Big fellow like that, smells of dry pine, dances better than the town folk, and took that cub straight into the trees. If I cross his tracks out there, I won't mind walking slow.
T1-OPEN-2-HOME-B: Thistle [sly]: Warm as a hayrick, knows his steps on the boards, and went right back to Lavinia with the little one tucked in safe. Grandda says a creature who keeps his temper on a chain is rarer than gold.
T1-OPEN-2-WOODS-B: Thistle [sly]: Warm, broad-shouldered, smells right, and smart enough to trade a stage for the deep woods with that cub. If he ever wants company that doesn't hold a chain, he's mine.
T1-OPEN-3A: Thistle [angry]: Stop grinning like a fox in a hen-coop. You breathe a word of this to Wren and I'll put burrs in your bedroll.
T1-OPEN-3B: Thistle [afraid]: Bark and bones, don't look at me like that. Keep your mouth shut around the others, hear?
T1-TEASE: A: > Should I buy you a tambourine and a velvet vest? | Thistle [smile]: Bark and bones, shut your trap! Take a pine cone to the ear and see how you dance. || B: > At least he wouldn't complain about sleeping on the roof. | Thistle [smile]: Ha! Take that pine cone and choke on it, you loud-mouthed crow.
T1-LUCKY: A: > Any bear with sense would be lucky to have you, Thistle. | Thistle [smile]: ...Hmph. Well, I know where the good berries grow, anyhow. || B: > He could look all over these woods and not do better. | Thistle [neutral]: ...You're just talking so I'll take first watch. Still, wouldn't mind sharing a salmon with him.
T1-PROMISE: A: > My lips are sealed, I promise. | Thistle [sly]: Words are wind; spit on a dry stone and swear by your boots like Grandda taught me. Break it and the crows get your Supper. || B: > Not a word to anyone, I swear it. | Thistle [neutral]: Swear it proper then, thumb to the bark and eye on the fire. Grandda says a camp oath holds till the ashes go cold.
T2-ASK-A: Wren [smile]: Met a girl with curling horns on a river-road once, lugging a lute half her size and a song she couldn't finish. Help me patch a last verse onto it before the damp gets in my throat, yeah?
T2-ASK-B: Wren [weary]: Old Master Sorrel said unfinished tunes draw moths, and I've been humming a half-made ballad from a horned girl I knew far from here. Give me three lines for the end of it—I'll allow it if they're terrible.
L1: hopeful: We walk the mist until the morning light, | grim: We march like ghosts into the starving night, | silly: We tripped on roots and gave the owls a fright,
L2: hopeful: With faithful lanterns burning warm and bright, | grim: Where every shadow sharpens for a fight, | silly: While arguing whose boots are laced too tight,
L3: hopeful: And side by side we keep the road in sight. | grim: And only fools and friends survive the blight. | silly: And trade the gloom for supper and a bite.
T2-SING-A: Narrator: {name} listens as Wren taps a heel against a blackened log and lets the last note rise with the woodsmoke. For three breaths even the pines stop dripping, and then the camp breaks into rough applause.
T2-SING-B: Narrator: You watch the firelight catch the brass pegs of the lute while Wren's clear voice settles over the wet grass. The quiet holds until a log splits in the embers, and then everyone around the fire cheers at once.
T2-AFTER-A: Wren [smile]: Easy—told you we'd make a proper tune of it! | Wren [sad]: Wherever that horned girl got to, I hope somebody helped her finish hers too.
T2-AFTER-B: Wren [sly]: Watch this, we'll be famous from here to the nearest ditch. | Wren [weary]: Still, wherever she is down the road, I hope someone finished the song for her too.
INN-A: Narrator: Downstairs, a squinting fiddler saws through Wren's tune a half-step flat, yet every wet cloak in the taproom thumps a mug and roars out the final line together.
INN-B: Narrator: Below the floorboards, a tavern lute mangles Wren's melody until the whole smoky room rises to bellow the last line into the rafters.
